leaves.title: Numbers 0–10
leaves.lessonBody: The numbers zero to ten in English: zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
commonMistakes: Do not confuse 'six' and 'sixty' — they sound different.

exercises.title: Write the number
exercises.instructions: Read the number word and type the digit.

exercises.title: Say the next number
exercises.instructions: Choose the number that comes next.

leaves.title: Numbers 11–100 and phone numbers
leaves.lessonBody: Numbers eleven to twenty have their own words (eleven, twelve, thirteen...). From twenty on, numbers combine a tens word (twenty, thirty, forty...) with a ones word (twenty-one, thirty-five). Phone numbers are read digit by digit, e.g. 608-5713 = six oh eight, five seven one three.
examples: My phone number is six one two, five five five, oh two oh six.
There are thirty students in the class.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse 'thirteen' (13) and 'thirty' (30) — the stress is different.
Phone numbers are read one digit at a time, not as a whole number.

exercises.title: Write the number
exercises.instructions: Read the number word and type the digit(s).

exercises.title: Choose the correct number word
exercises.instructions: Choose the word that matches the number.

leaves.title: Days of the week
leaves.lessonBody: The seven days of the week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Days of the week always start with a capital letter.
examples: My English class is on Monday.
The weekend is Saturday and Sunday.
commonMistakes: Do not write days with a lowercase letter — 'monday' is wrong, write 'Monday'.

exercises.title: Complete with the correct day
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct day of the week.

questions.prompt: If today is Monday, tomorrow is ___.
If today is Thursday, tomorrow is ___.
The two weekend days are Saturday and ___.

exercises.title: Which day comes next?
exercises.instructions: Choose the day that comes after the one shown.

leaves.title: Countries
leaves.lessonBody: Common country names in English, always written with a capital letter: Brazil, Canada, China, Egypt, Japan, Mexico, Peru, Spain, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the United States, Vietnam.
commonMistakes: Country names always start with a capital letter.
'the United States' and 'the United Kingdom' both need 'the' before them.

exercises.title: Complete with the correct country
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct country name.

leaves.title: Nationalities
leaves.lessonBody: Nationality words are adjectives formed from country names, e.g. Brazil → Brazilian, Japan → Japanese, Canada → Canadian. The stress is usually on the same syllable as the country name, but not always — Japan → Japanese moves the stress.
commonMistakes: Nationality words are always capitalized, like country names.
Some nationality endings are irregular: Japan → Japanese (not 'Japanian'), not a simple '+n' or '+ian' pattern for every country.

exercises.title: Complete with the correct nationality
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the nationality that matches the country.

exercises.title: Match the country to the nationality
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct nationality for the country shown.

leaves.title: Classroom objects
leaves.lessonBody: Common classroom objects: a board, a door, a window, a chair, a table, a laptop, a dictionary, a pen, a bag, a piece of paper.
examples: Open your dictionary to page ten.
commonMistakes: 'a' is used before consonant sounds (a board, a chair); 'an' before vowel sounds (an umbrella).

exercises.title: Complete with a or an
exercises.instructions: Complete each phrase with a or an.

exercises.title: Choose the correct object
exercises.instructions: Choose the object that matches the description.
